text: Mangroves are a complex group containing some 70 species. They range from low shrubs to 60-meter-high timber trees. Though most prolific in Southeast Asia, mangroves circle the Earth in a band within 30 degrees of the Equator. Wherever they grow, they're brilliant at coping with hostile environments. Although salt can inhibit plant growth, each mangrove has an ultrafiltration system to keep out much of the salt from sea water. Mangroves also have complex root systems that allow them to survive in the intertidal zone. Some have snorkel-like roots called pneumatophores that stick out of the mud to help them take in air; others use prop roots to keep their trunks upright in the soft sediment at the tide's edge.

text: These plants are forces to be reckoned with. Their interlocking roots stop riverborne sediments from flowing out to sea, and their trunks and branches serve as a valuable defensive 'fence' that absorbs the power of waves during storms. Yet mangroves have been cut down in many countries to make way for a range of developments. Since mangrove forests act as natural breakwaters, mitigating property damage and perhaps saving lives, the logic of allowing a country's mangrove 'bioshields' to be destroyed is being questioned.

By planting mangroves, it has gained over 120,000 hectares of new land on the Bay of Bengal. These plantings are relatively new, but there have been mangroves in the region for thousands of years. text: One of the greatest threats to mangroves comes from shrimp farming. At first glance, shrimp might seem the perfect export. Rich countries have an insatiable appetite for this shellfish, and the developing world has the available land and right climate to farm it. Unfortunately, a prime location for shrimp ponds also happens to be the shore zone occupied by mangroves. To make matters worse, shrimp farmers typically abandon their ponds after a few crop cycles (to avoid disease outbreaks and declining productivity) and move to a different site, destroying more mangroves as they go.

text: For more than 25 years, Jin Eong Ong, a retired professor of marine and coastal studies in Penang, Malaysia, has been investigating what role these forests might play in climate change. Ong and his colleagues have been looking at the carbon budget of mangroves — the balance sheet that compares all the carbon inputs and outputs of the mangrove ecosystem. They have found that these forests are highly effective carbon 'sinks' — mangroves absorb carbon dioxide, taking carbon out of circulation and cutting down on the amount of greenhouse gas emitted. If mangroves were to become recognized as carbon-storage assets, that could radically alter the way these forests are valued, says Ong. If carbon trading becomes a reality — that is, if forest-rich, carbon-absorbing countries are able to sell so-called emissions credits to more industrialized, carbon-emitting countries — it could at the least, prolong the life of mangroves.

text: On the African coast, a different mangrove experiment is happening. In Eritrea, men are knocking the bottoms out of empty cans. Nearby, on the shores of the Red Sea, women push the hollow cans into the soft sediment. Into each one, the women press a mangrove seed or propagule. This is the brainchild of cell biologist Gordon Sato. Since water is such a scarce resource here, Sato wanted to develop some form of salt-water-based agriculture. Mangroves occur naturally, though patchily, by the Red Sea; they flourish in salt water, and camels eat their leaves. So, why not grow more mangroves and feed the foliage to livestock like sheep? He began planting and failed. All the saplings died. Undaunted, Sato looked closely at places where mangroves grew, and noticed they occurred only where fresh water was channeled during the brief rains that fall in this region. Sato reasoned it was not fresh water the trees needed but minerals the water brings from inland. By conducting some simple trials, Sato and his colleagues assessed how much of these minerals mangrove seedlings need, and devised a low-tech method of supplying them. When the propagules are planted, a small amount of iron is buried alongside. So, too, is a small bag with holes punched in containing a fertilizer rich in nitrogen and phosphorus.

text: After a few years, Sato's project began to succeed: 700,000 mangroves are now growing on the formerly treeless shore. The mangrove mud is sprouting roots. Oysters have started to cling to them, and crab trails crisscross the sediment. Fishermen have started to catch small species such as mullet. And the little fish that make the mangroves their home attract bigger, predatory fish that sell for good prices. However, there is still work to do. Sato has started using sheep to fine-tune the livestock-rearing side of the scheme, but has found that mangrove leaves and propagules, though highly nutritious, do not provide a complete range of vitamins and minerals. He believes fish meal will provide the missing nutrients, and visualizes a pen of livestock beside every house. Who would have imagined it: the mangrove as the foundation of prosperity!
